In 2005, a group of Russian, American and Indian zoologists published an analysis of historical and contemporary data on body weights of wild and captive tigers, both female and male across all subspecies. The data used include weights of tigers that were older than 35 months and measured in the presence of authors. Their comparison with historical data indicates that up to the first half of the 20th century both male and female Siberian tigers were on average heavier than post-1970 ones. The average historical wild male Siberian tiger weighed 215.3 kg (475 lb) and the female 137.5 kg (303 lb); the contemporary wild male Siberian tiger weighs 176.4 kg (389 lb) on average with an asymptotic limit being 222.3 kg (490 lb); a wild female weighs 117.9 kg (260 lb) on average. Historical Siberian tigers and Bengal tigers were the largest ones, whereas contemporary Siberian tigers are on average lighter than Bengal tigers.

Well there’s a small correction:
That “lion has 58.8% muscle mass highest among mammals” actually comes from Davis (1962). In that study, only two lions were measured:

One had 62.5% muscle with just 5.7% fat (a very lean lioness)

The other had 55% muscle, but the fat percentage wasn’t specified.


A newer 2017 study (Palaeontologia Electronica) found 57.1% muscle, including about 13% fat, which gives a more realistic number.

So technically, lions are second, because bobcats were measured at 58.5% muscle — the highest recorded among cats so far.

Measured muscle mass (% of body weight):

1.  Bobcat – 58.5%


2.  Lion – 57.1%


3. Lynx – 56.5%


4.  Tiger – 56% (healthy specimen)


5.  Cheetah – 50%


6.  Domestic cat – 47%



And since jaguars and leopards haven’t had their total muscle mass officially measured or published yet, there’s a real chance one of them could actually have the highest once proper data comes out.
